clue.text: Geriatric's party I'm a bit annoyed about

definitions.note: the 's stands for 'is', joining the definition to the wordplay; a geriatric here is a doddering old person

parts.note: a do is an informal word for a party

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the exclamation is read backwards

parts.note: 'drat!' is the mild exclamation of someone a bit annoyed

explanation.surface: An old person's party, about which the speaker is mildly irritated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'm a bit annoyed' stands for the mild oath 'drat!', and 'about' makes TARD of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe an old person whose faculties are failing, a senile oldster.

clue.text: One'll break faith with failing soldiers

parts.note: a defect is a failing or flaw
OR, other ranks, is the usual abbreviation for ordinary soldiers

explanation.surface: Someone who betrays their side because of the soldiers' failures.
explanation.definitionFit: A turncoat abandons allegiance to their country or cause, breaking faith with it.

clue.text: Those visiting solicitors holding teacher up

indicators.note: holding means the first piece wraps round the second

parts.note: touts are people who solicit custom, not lawyers here

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: sir is how pupils address a male teacher

explanation.surface: Lawyers who are visiting, keeping a schoolteacher hoisted aloft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Solicitors' suggests lawyers, but here they are people touting for custom; 'up' makes RIS in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Sightseers are people who are visiting a place, which is what holidaymakers do.

clue.text: Airline lady's mounted remedial course

indicators.note: in a down clue, mounted means raised up, so the letters read upwards

parts.note: BA is British Airways
her is the possessive pronoun for a lady

explanation.surface: An airline stewardess has climbed aboard for a corrective course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mounted' reverses BAHER in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for rehabilitation, a programme of treatment helping someone recover, often from addiction.

clue.text: Landowner introducing married daughter was embarrassed

indicators.note: introducing means bringing the second piece inside the first

parts.note: a squire is the chief landowner of an English village

explanation.surface: A landowner presenting his married daughter felt awkward.
explanation.definitionFit: To wriggle with discomfort is what someone does when ill at ease or ashamed.

clue.text: Barman, in short, quite contrary to start with

definitions.text: Barman, in short, quite contrary to start with

parts.words: Barman, in short, quite contrary to start with
parts.note: a barman is a barrister, a member of the Bar; his title in short is QC, and those letters start the words quite contrary

explanation.surface: A bartender who, as the nursery rhyme's Mary does, behaves awkwardly from the outset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barman' is not a pub worker but a member of the Bar. Senior barristers are abbreviated QC, and Q and C are the first letters of 'quite contrary'.
explanation.definitionFit: Senior British barristers appointed under a queen bear this title, usually shortened to the initials QC.

clue.text: Individual approaching home with zeal

parts.note: I is one, a single individual
near means approaching or close by
a nest is a bird's home

explanation.surface: Someone getting close to home, keenly.
explanation.definitionFit: To act seriously and with determination is to show enthusiasm, the idiom for real sincerity.

clue.text: Mum wearing extremely leaky overall

parts.note: ma is an informal word for mum
you are in clothes you are wearing

indicators.note: extremely means taking the extreme letters, first and last, of leaky

explanation.surface: Mother is dressed in a dripping overall, a piece of protective clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overall' looks like a garment but is the definition, an adverb.
explanation.definitionFit: Largely or for the most part is the sense of overall as an adverb summing things up.

clue.text: Study comes to an end, keeping good time

indicators.note: keeping means holding the next piece inside

parts.note: something that dies comes to an end

explanation.surface: A piece of research finishes on schedule.
explanation.definitionFit: To absorb and think over information is to take it in thoroughly, as when you mull over a report.

clue.text: Finish job in WC and look embarrassed

definitions.meaning: pulling the chain or lever to send water through the toilet bowl finishes the job
to go red in the face, blushing

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both clearing a lavatory with water and reddening with shame.

clue.text: Travelling kings were sticking together, one might say

indicators.note: travelling means the letters move about into a new order

explanation.surface: Royals on tour stuck together, as you might put it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Travelling' rearranges KINGS WERE. 'one might say' flags a loose, playful definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Spearing food on a kebab spike pins the pieces together, a humorous take on sticking things.

clue.text: No Etonian detected at USA gathering?

indicators.note: gathering means the letters are collected and assembled into a new order

explanation.surface: Was someone spotted at an American meeting not an Old Etonian?
explanation.walkthrough: 'gathering' rearranges DETECTED AT USA. Eton is Britain's most famous private (fee-paying) school, so a non-Etonian may have gone to a free school.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone schooled by the government system rather than privately did not attend Eton, the famous fee-paying school.

clue.text: Forged bill in M&S or Aldi, say, a source of irritation

indicators.note: in puts the reworked letters inside the other piece

parts.note: Marks & Spencer and Aldi are examples of a chain of shops

indicators.note: forged means the letters are fabricated into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A counterfeit banknote turns up at a supermarket and causes annoyance.
explanation.walkthrough: M&S (Marks & Spencer) and Aldi are British supermarket chains. 'Forged' yields ILBL.
explanation.definitionFit: An itchy, inflamed swelling on fingers or toes caused by cold, so literally a cause of irritation.

clue.text: Slight setback hampering European policies

indicators.note: hampering means getting in the way, so the letter sits inside
setback here means the word is set back, read in reverse

parts.note: a slur is a slight or insult

explanation.surface: A minor reverse holds up European policies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'setback' reverses SLUR to RULS; 'hampering' puts E inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Regulations and principles governing conduct are policies an organisation lays down.

clue.text: Fashion etc, the Tudors extended

indicators.note: fashion as a verb means to shape, so the letters are reshaped

explanation.surface: Tudor clothing and the like grew longer and longer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fashion' looks like a noun about clothes; it is the verb rearranging ETC THE TUDORS.
explanation.definitionFit: Arms or limbs reaching out at full length are stretched out, spread to their full extent.

clue.text: Inscrutable type — he's quiet during lean times

indicators.note: during means within, so the pieces go inside

parts.note: lean means thin
taken as written, without the apostrophe
P is piano, the musical direction for quiet
X is the multiplication sign, times

explanation.surface: A poker-faced person keeps silent through hard times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lean times' suggests hardship; 'lean' gives THIN and 'times' gives X separately.
explanation.definitionFit: The Egyptian monument with a lion's body and human face is a byword for enigmatic, unreadable people.

clue.text: He'll judge about six sheep, first in ring

parts.note: re means about or concerning
VI is six in Roman numerals
a ewe is a female sheep

indicators.note: first in means the opening letter of the next word

explanation.surface: A show judge assesses roughly half a dozen sheep, the first in the ring.
explanation.definitionFit: A critic assesses and evaluates plays, books or films, passing judgment on them.

clue.text: Mobile characters in Tate don't care for?

indicators.note: mobile means movable, so the letters in the words are moved into a new order

explanation.surface: Do people dislike the mobiles displayed in the Tate gallery?
explanation.walkthrough: The Tate is London's group of national art galleries; a mobile is a hanging sculpture. 'Mobile' rearranges TATE DONT.
explanation.definitionFit: To look after or deal with someone or something is to take care of them.

clue.text: After study, no women find time for revision

indicators.note: after study means the remaining pieces follow the word for study

parts.note: to read a subject is to study it at university
just men means only males, with no women

explanation.surface: Following their studies, the all-male group find time to revise.
explanation.definitionFit: Making an adjustment again is a revision, an alteration or correction to something.

clue.text: Loose car part regularly fixed in hour by champ

indicators.note: regularly means taking every other letter, here the first, third, fifth and so on

explanation.surface: A wobbly component fixed in an hour by an expert mechanic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fixed in' merely links; 'regularly' takes alternate letters of HOUR BY CHAMP.
explanation.definitionFit: The metal disc covering a wheel's centre is a car part notorious for coming off.

clue.text: Nutmeg's stopping show in German city

indicators.note: stopping means plugging a gap, so the piece goes inside

parts.note: to wear a look is to show it, as in wearing a smile
the setter Nutmeg speaking of herself: Nutmeg is, I'm

explanation.surface: The setter features in an exhibition held in a German city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nutmeg' is this puzzle's setter, so 'Nutmeg's' becomes I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: This city in Thuringia gave its name to the 1919–33 republic and was home to Goethe.

clue.text: Run through museum unclothed, ending in shop

indicators.note: unclothed means stripped of the outer letters, leaving the middle
ending in means the last letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: A streaker dashes through a museum naked and finishes up in the gift shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run' looks like streaking; it is the definition, exhaust.
explanation.definitionFit: To exhaust a supply is to consume it completely, running through it until nothing is left.

clue.text: Abandoned rebel leader probed by secret police

indicators.note: probed by means the second piece pokes into the first

parts.note: Jack Cade led the Kentish rebellion of 1450
the Stasi were East Germany's secret police

explanation.surface: An insurgent chief, investigated by secret police, has been left alone.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack Cade led a revolt against Henry VI in 1450; the Stasi were East Germany's secret police.
explanation.definitionFit: Something discarded or rejected has been thrown away, dropped and left behind.

clue.text: Beyond a double bend, river's clear blue

indicators.note: beyond means the river comes after the earlier pieces

parts.note: the letter Z looks like a double bend, as on road signs
the Ure is a Yorkshire river; the 's is 'is', linking to the definition

explanation.surface: Past an S-bend, the river runs a limpid blue.
explanation.walkthrough: Z resembles a double-bend road sign. The Ure is a river in Yorkshire, England.
explanation.definitionFit: Cerulean, the bright blue of a cloudless sky, is the colour this word names.

clue.text: Order to confine gangster for last two members of panel

indicators.note: for means in place of, here replacing the final pair of letters

parts.note: a committee is a panel of members
Al Capone is the archetypal gangster

explanation.surface: An instruction to lock up a mobster, issued for two final members of a panel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for last two' replaces the final EE of COMMITTEE with AL, from Al Capone.
explanation.definitionFit: A court's formal order sending someone to prison or a hospital confines them.

clue.text: Single global enterprise returned early deposit

parts.note: the UN, the United Nations, is a worldwide undertaking

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: dew is deposited on the ground early in the morning

explanation.surface: One worldwide company gave back an advance payment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'early deposit' suggests banking; it is morning dew, reversed by 'returned'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone not married is single, without a spouse.

clue.text: Without us, Oedipus Rex collapsed — shock treatment applied

indicators.note: without means the letters of the word us are excluded from the pool
collapsed means the letters fall into disorder and are rearranged

explanation.surface: Sophocles' tragedy fell apart without us, so drastic remedies were brought in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without us' removes U and S from OEDIPUS REX; 'collapsed' rearranges the rest. 'shock' is a mass of hair, not a jolt.
explanation.definitionFit: Hydrogen bleach used to lighten hair is a treatment for a shock, a thick mop of hair.

clue.text: Dam with added function, not the conventional sort

indicators.note: with added means the second piece is tacked on after the first

parts.note: a weir is a low dam across a river
a do is a party or function

explanation.surface: A dam given an extra purpose is unusual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'function' looks like purpose; it is a social event, DO.
explanation.definitionFit: An eccentric or oddball person, someone strange and unusual in behaviour.
